title: TB0-01070
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXX (the claimant), is a citizen of the People's Republic of China, who claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant alleged that after he was rejected by a girlfriend in mid 2007 he became very distraught with his life. The claimant's friend, XXXXXXXX, learned of this and introduced the claimant to Roman Catholicism, eventually taking him to attend an underground Roman Catholic church in his home area starting in early XXXXXX 2008. The claimant attended this church with approximately fifteen members every week from then until it was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) at XXXX 2009, (XXXXX).

The claimant and one other person were apprehended by the PSB on that occasion. During his week in detention the claimant was interrogated, beaten, and tortured by the officers. He was released on condition that he would not engage in any further illegal house church activities, and his family paid a fine.

Upon his release the claimant was initially concerned about resuming any church activities, but after he called his friend in XXX 2009 he re-joined the group. However, the PSB raided the group meeting a second time, on XXXXXX, 2009. This time the claimant was able to escape and fled into hiding. Subsequently he learned that the PSB went to his home to look for him on XXXX XX, 2009, questioned his parents, seized his Resident Identity Card, searched the house, and accused him of being involved in illegal religious activities. The PSB also left a summons with his parents. He later learned that three members of his congregation had been arrested, including his friend, XXXXXXXX. He arranged to leave China and arrived in Canada on XXXXXXX, 2009.

The PSB has continued to come to his home looking for him. The claimant fears that if he returned to China he would be arrested and jailed, and he adds that he cannot practice his religion as freely in China as he can in Canada.

The claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China is established by documentation provided to the panel by the claimant, specifically, the claimant's household register or hukou2 as tendered into evidence. I note that I do have strong reservations in this area, but not enough to rebut the presumption that the claimant's testimony is credible in reference to identity as an alleged citizen of China.

Specifically, for reasons noted below, I do not find that the claimant's testimony that his house church was ever raided is credible and trustworthy, and thus I do not find that there was ever any PSB interest in him, or that they came to his home and seized his Chinese Resident Identity Card (RIC). Consequently, I determine that his testimony about the loss of his RIC is not credible.
The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection for the following reasons.

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's PIF3 narrative and his oral testimony concerning his membership in an underground church and his pursuit by agents of the PSB. I find that the claimant was not a credible witness in this regard and is not currently wanted for arrest by the PSB on account of his religious activities in China. As well, I find that should the claimant return to Fujian province in China and should he practice Roman Catholicism there, there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted in Fujian province for that practice.

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age (40), education, and background in China. He alleges that he has only eight years of education in China. In addition, the panel took into account the milieu of the hearing room, cultural factors, and the anxiety a claimant may feel in responding to viva voce examination through an interpreter. CREDIBILITY The Church Closure

The claimant alleged in his oral testimony that his underground church ceased all activities after XXXXX, 2009 until XXX 2009 due to fear of the authorities. He also stated that he personally rejoined in late XXX. However, his PIF narrative says nothing about the church itself closing or ceasing activities at this time. I asked him why not. He replied that at the time he wrote his PIF he had just come to Canada, he was very nervous, and for some events it was hard to explain clearly.

I do not accept any of his explanations. The PIF narrative instructions ask that one explain all significant events, including those affecting other similarly situated persons. If the church had been forced to close for two or three months due to fear of PSB action that is a significant restriction on the religious freedom of other members of his church. At all material times, including completion of his PIF, the claimant has had benefit of competent legal counsel to assist him, so in my view there is no reasonable excuse for such an omission if, in fact, his church had ever closed. I draw a negative credibility inference. The Threat to His Parents

The claimant alleged in his oral testimony that his parents had been threatened by the PSB with unspecified punishment. He said this was because they thought his parents knew where he was. However, his PIF narrative did not mention any such threats so I asked him why not. He replied that this sort of thing is very common in China.

Again, the narrative instructions direct claimant's to note any measures taken against members of one's family. If his family had been threatened as alleged it would have been important to mention as any PSB threat in China would be very worrisome to any individual in that country due to the power vested in the PSB. He has not done so and his excuse is insufficient; whether such is common in China or not is unimportant to the panel. I draw a negative credibility inference. The PSB Summons

The claimant also entered a document entitled, "summons"4 that he has alleged was left with his parents after the second raid on his church. The documentary evidence5 regarding the issuance of a summons notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or family member. However, it was also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members, instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. Though this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable. The documentary evidence6 also notes the format and appearance of summonses. It is stated that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect. The summons presented by the claimant at his hearing does not include any section that is an acknowledgment that the summons was received.

The absence of an acknowledgment section is not consistent with the documentary evidence. As noted above, a summons is either issued to the person named in the summons or to a family or household member and the person who receives the summons is expected to sign in that regard. There is no signature or acknowledgment of receipt of any kind on the summons provided by the claimant.

Furthermore, I note that the claimant's summons did not identify his address, age, or gender on the face of the document, which is not consistent with the sample document in the National Documentation Package.7
The claimant was given an opportunity to explain why there was no address on the face of the PSB Summons, and it lacked the other features noted, and he responded, "I don't know how to explain."

I have considered the statement in Response to Information Request CHN42444.E 8(the "RIR") which identifies two types of summonses: Zhaunhaun, which is used to summon a suspect for questioning without arrest, and Juzhaun, an arrest-summons. The RIR states the Zhaunhaun summons for someone to appear for interrogation must state the person, time, and place of appearance for questioning. The duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect who keeps one copy. The same RIR goes on to attach samples of an arrest warrant, an arrest-summons for interrogation and a notice of summons to testify but not the Zhaunhaun summons.9

The claimant testified that the police only left the summons with his parents on XXXXXX, 2009, after he had been arrested in April of the same year for church activities and released on signing an agreement that he would no longer participate in such activities, and after three other church members had already been arrested during the XXXXXX, 2009 raid.

According to the RIR, Zhaunhaun (summons) is used when no arrest or detention of suspects is necessary or contemplated, i.e. when cooperation is expected or flight is not likely. See Art. 92 of PRC Criminal Procedure Law. This is not a coercive measure (qiang zhi cuoshi). (Emphasis added). However, the claimant's testimony would suggest that his arrest was both necessary and contemplated by the PSB, so in my view this would rule out use of the Zhaunhaun.

Instead, a Juzhuan (arrest summons) would most likely be used in such circumstances "when voluntary compliance is not appropriate or Zhaunhaun has failed. See Article 50 of PRC Criminal Procedure Law and Article 60 of Public Security Criminal Procedure Regulations. This is a coercive measure (qiang zhi cuoshi)."10 Given the claimant's allegation that three members of his house church had been arrested and that the PSB were intent on arresting him for the second time, it is reasonable to expect an investigation had been conducted and that the PSB would have issued a Juzhuan summons (Arrest-Summon for Interrogation). a. The documentary evidence provided an example of the Juzhuan summons and notes the information that is to be included on the portion of a summons left with the person or family members of the person named in the summons. It states that the summons should include, among other things, the following statement: According to PRC Criminal Procedure Law Article 45, it has been decided that investigator from this bureau (name) will effectuate arrest at the resident (address) of (named person). b. The documentary evidence also notes that the summons would include the date issued and the date on which the summons was served on the person and the person's signature. The summons tendered by the claimant does not contain his address nor is the date of service indicated. The summons also does not bear the signature of either of the claimant's parents despite his testimony that they were the persons on whom the summons was served. The summons also does not bear the statement "according to PRC Criminal Law Procedure Article 45", instead it refers to regulation 92. Additionally, the claimant's summons states, "You are required to report at 10:15 on XXXX, 2009 to Criminal Division of the Public Security Bureau of XXXXXX City for enquiry", but does not identify the address that the claimant was to report to or whether it is "am or pm". As detailed below, an area as large as this would certainly have multiple PSB offices and the panel concludes it is reasonable that a specific office would be indicated.
The claimant was given an opportunity to address the discrepancies on the face of the PSB Summons and responded, "I don't know".

The claimant is from XXXXX, which has a population of approximately seven hundred and fifty thousand, and there are over thirty-seven million people in the province.11 It is reasonable to assume that the police force of a large and populous area such as this would be well versed with regard to the information that would be required for the effective service and procedures associated with the issuance of summonses. By relying on common sense and rationale, in the panel's opinion, it is reasonable to assume that the PSB document would include the address of the person named on the summons, since this information would be required by the serving officer(s) to correctly identify the location of the individual's known address to effect service of the document. The Panel determines that it is neither reasonable nor credible that the summons would not identify the correct PRC Criminal Law Procedure information or the claimant's address on the face of the document. The panel notes from the documentary evidence that fraudulent documents, including summonses are easily acquired in China.12

The panel has considered the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant compared to the documentary evidence, as well as, the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the summons provided by the claimant is not a genuine document and the claimant has deliberately attempted to mislead the panel by proffering a fraudulent document as evidence to support his refugee claim and substantiate his PIF narrative. For these same reasons, the panel further determines that the claimant is not wanted by the PSB for any alleged involvement in any underground house church. The panel notes that this analysis regarding deficiencies in PSB summons documents has recently been recently considered by the Federal Court in two separate instances and found not to be unreasonable.13

Having found that the claimant is not being pursued by the PSB, the panel finds that the claimant was not a practicing Catholic in China as he alleges. The panel further finds that the claimant's allegation that he was a practicing Catholic in China, is not credible and was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim and that these credibility findings raise a significant doubt about his general credibility.

Having found that the claimant was not a Catholic in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine practicing Catholic in this country. In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution which did not exist cannot be said to belong to this category.14 [29] The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, including the negative credibility inferences drawn regarding the important omissions in his PIF narrative, that the claimant joined a Catholic church in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. In the context as noted above, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed the panel finds that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Catholic, nor would he be perceived to be in China. [30] I give little or no weight to any church letter, or certificates of Baptism or confirmation.15 These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they can not attest to his true motivation. [31] Again, I note from the documentary evidence that fraudulent documents, including summonses are easily acquired in China. 16 I conclude, on a balance of probabilities, that the Detention Release Notice, Payment Receipt and list of Items Confiscated,17 are also fraudulent documents and give them no weight. Medical Report [32] The claimant provided the panel with a report from a physician, Dr. XXXX, dated XXXXXXX, 2011,18 which states that the claimant has a scar on his XXXXXX consistent with allegations of torture by the PSB. The panel accepts that the claimant may have been injured and suffered a scar as described in the report but the panel is not persuaded that this is related to the issues or events alleged in this claim. I do not otherwise find that his testimony was credible or trustworthy regarding the alleged arrest by the PSB, so I do not give the report much weight. [33] I find, moreover, that any discussion therein of any mental upset on the part of the claimant has limited evidentiary value as it was based on one interview and self-reporting of the claimant's situation and symptoms. In addition, there was no interpreter present and the examination took place "on the basis of Mr. XXXX limited English,"19 as Dr. XXXX notes. The claimant used an interpreter for his PIF and at his refugee hearing. [34] I give this report little or no evidentiary weight. I also note in any event that the PIF narrative, while stating that he was "sometimes beaten and tortured"20 by the PSB officers while in detention, made no mention that they directly applied a hot iron rod to his XXX leaving a lasting eight centimeter long scar as Dr. XXXX suggests. I would have expected that matter should have been highlighted in the PIF narrative if it had truly been caused by the PSB, as it is no mere detail, and a general assertion of torture pales by comparison. Arrest of Fellow Church Members and Pursuit of Claimant by the PSB [35] The claimant testified that following the first PSB raid in XXXX 2009, he and one other of the fifteen attendees at the house church meeting were arrested and questioned, he personally was tortured including the application of a hot iron on his XXXX leaving a scar, and that at the second raid in XXXXXX 2009 three others were arrested. In his oral evidence, he was asked what he knew about the three subsequently. He said that he learned that they were still being detained as of the date of his refugee hearing, over two years later. [36] His testimony in these regards, about multiple detentions of lay persons, raids on house churches and abuse and torture of attendees, runs counter to the country condition documents that will be demonstrated later in these reasons with the analysis of the Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province. In this regard, the panel draws a negative inference. [37] The claimant also alleges that the PSB have attended his home on fourteen occasions with the intent of arresting him, and that when they went there on XXXXXX, 2009 they gave his parents a summons for him to report.21 [38] On the basis of the subsequent analysis on the Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province and in the context of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's allegation that there were two raids on his house church, and that in the first, he was detained with one other person and subsequently tortured and left scarred, and that in the second, three of his fellow church members were arrested and each has been detained for over two years, is neither plausible nor credible. Having found that the claimant's testimony about his arrest and the arrest and incarceration of his fellow church members is not credible, the panel further finds that the alleged raids on the claimant's house church did not occur. [39] The claimant was asked a number of questions concerning Catholicism and the Bible. While he demonstrated some knowledge, it does not necessarily mean he is a genuine practicing Catholic. Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province [40] Notwithstanding the forgoing analysis, alternatively, if the claimant decides to become a genuine Catholic and practice his faith upon return to China, the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for practicing Catholicism in an unregistered church. [41] In dealing with the issue of repression of Catholics in Fujian province, the panel has examined the documentary evidence closely. Although precise figures are difficult to obtain, documentation22 highlights: The Catholic Patriotic Association (CPA) reports that 5.3 million persons worship in its churches, and it is estimated that there are an additional 12 million or more persons who worship in unregistered Catholic churches that do not affiliate with the CPA. According to official sources, the government-sanctioned Catholic Patriotic Association has more than 70 bishops, almost 3,000 priests and nuns, 6,000 churches and meeting places, and 12 seminaries. There are thought to be approximately 40 bishops operating "underground," some of whom are in prison or under house arrest. [42] With respect to Fujian province, where the claimant is from, according to a report in the Times of London, the Catholic Church is strong there and most of the faithful are loyal to Rome.23 The panel acknowledges that sporadic persecution of the "underground" Catholic Church occurs. There are references to Catholic clergy being forced into hiding, jailed or detained, placed under surveillance and detentions, pressure being applied by Chinese authorities for Catholic clergy and laypersons to renounce ordinations approved by the Vatican and join the CPA or face fines, job loss, or detention and having children barred from school.24 According to one source as of March 2007, five bishops and 14 priests belonging to the "underground" church were in prison, eight bishops were under house arrest or surveillance and two others were in hiding.25 The documentation26 identifies that the treatment of Catholics, within the "unofficial" church, varies from place to place. It is local politics that dictate the final outcome of religious policy and the implementation of the Chinese Communist Party on freedom of religious belief can range from endorsement of religion to suppression. [43] Asia Harvest, an inter-denominational Christian ministry working in China, estimates that there are over a million Roman or house church Catholics in Fujian province, including over 20,000 Roman Catholics in the claimant's home area of XXXXX,27 as well as, over 900, 000 who are involved with the state-sanctioned Catholic Patriotic Association church. [44] There is mixed information regarding the treatment of Christians in Fujian province. Several sources stated that they believed that authorities in Guangdong and Fujian provinces might be more tolerant than those in other Chinese provinces. The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council expressed the opinion that officials in Guangdong and Fujian provinces have good relations with government-recognized bishops and have allowed non-official bishops to operate openly.28 Conversely, a newspaper article refers to Fujian as one of the provinces where the most Catholics are located and that they are [translation] "tightly controlled" by local authorities. The President of the Cardinal Kung Foundation stated that Fujian province was one of "the worst" provinces for the "persecution" of the unofficial Catholic Church. [42] There are no diplomatic relationships existing currently between the Chinese Government and the Holy See. It is estimated that 90 percent of official Catholic bishops have reconciled with the Vatican. Many priests and bishops publicly acknowledged that the Vatican had approved their appointments. They suffered no punishment for this public stance. Pressure from the CPA on "unregistered" Catholic bishops to join the official church continued, and some unregistered priests and bishops were detained. [43] The State has declared that religious communities are important for the construction of a "harmonious society." From the perspective of the Holy See, there has been no declaration of a schism between any part of the Catholic Church in China and the Vatican.29 This is not to suggest that tensions do not exist between the Chinese government and the Holy See. Contentious issues surrounding the government's control of the selection of "patriotic" Chinese bishops and local officials cracking down on the "underground" church remain. [44] The panel is mindful that certain documentation30 indicates that the number of persecutory incidents may not be fully reflected in documentation and such factors as censorship in communications, failure to report cases of persecution for fear of retaliation by the government and the possibility that individuals in remote areas may have no idea that they can seek help from outside China can effect the number of reports. [45] In the case of the Catholic Church, there is information detailing very specific examples from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian province. There is even information from Fujian province that indicates to the panel that information regarding persecutory treatment against members of the Catholic faith is documented if it has occurred. Further, there are a number of observers, such as the Holy Spirit Study Centre, the Research Branch of the Diocese of Hong Kong (principally concerned with the situation of Catholics in mainland China), AsiaNews.it (which provides information on ecclesiastic communities in Asia), numerous news agencies, Cardinal Fung Foundation, and Freedom House31 to name a few. These observers strive to inform the world whenever any religious persecution takes place in China. [46] Arguably, the Roman Catholic Church itself has a vested interest in bringing to light any abhorrent human rights transgressions involving its adherents. [47] I give no weight to any documents from Boxun.com in counsel's documents32 as this is an open source website like Wikipedia33 where anyone may post articles regardless of their provenance. [48] In the 9 June 2010, telephone interview, with the IRB Research Directorate,34 Mr. Bob Fu, "the President of China Aid Association stated that east coast provinces are generally 'more open' with fewer incidents involving Christians reported to the CAA (CAA 9 June 2010). However, the CAA President also stated that this did not necessarily mean there were fewer incidents, but rather that they were not reported (ibid.)." [49] In reference to the claimant's particular allegations, in the panel's view, if two raids on the same small church of fifteen persons had occurred, and one individual (the claimant) left scarred by torture after the first detention, and there were a further three arrests with multi-year detentions of other Roman Catholic Churchgoers, such would be an example of an egregious situation and would reasonably be expected to appear in reports dealing with religious persecution amongst the multitude of different sources, which strive to inform the world of religious repression in China. [50] Given that information can flow to and from mainland China via means of personal contact, informal NGO networks, telephone calls, etc.; and, that in the past, there has been documentary evidence dealing with detention and arrests of Catholic bishops and priests, from Fujian and other more remote provinces; and, because of the large number of documentary sources that have a vested interest in highlighting any and all information that negatively impacts on religious freedom, the panel determines that it would be reasonable for it to have before it information of state actions taken against Catholic parishioners in Fujian province if any actions were taken, particularly in light of the sizable number of Roman Catholics estimated to be in Fujian. [51] The most recent documentary35 evidence provided to the Board reveals that underground priests have been arrested in Fujian in March 2010. Given the fact that information exists to show arrests of priests, it is reasonable to expect to see persuasive evidence that ordinary members of the Roman Catholic Church in Fujian province are facing persecution. Further, the availability of priests, nuns and lay catechists in the diocese associated with Fujian province persuades the panel that the claimant can return to Fujian and participate in the Roman Catholic church of her choosing. [52] The claimant testified that three fellow house church members were arrested and were ultimately sentenced to multi-year imprisonment. A close examination of the documentation regarding Catholic faithful in China clearly indicates that the harshest treatment is meted out to Bishops and Priests. In the case of Fujian province the most recent article indicates that the priests involved in organizing the camp for three hundred university students were detained for fifteen days and then released. Other priests involved in the matter were fined 500 Yuan. In terms of the totality of the evidence the alleged punishment given to the lay members of the claimant's church, who were arrested, is not in keeping with the types of punishment that has been referred to in the documentation with respect to non-Priests or Bishops. [53] Relying on documentary evidence that indicates millions of Catholic parishioners belong to the "unregistered" church and that the documentation in the context of the "unregistered" Catholic Church indicates, by far, that persecution occurs to bishops and priests. Further, there is extremely limited evidence of state authorities taking action against parishioners in Fujian province. In addition, Catholic congregations, worship freely. It is reasonable to expect that documentation from Fujian province indicating actions by state authorities against parishioners at the time of the alleged incident and more recently should be before the panel. In coming to this determination, the panel has been guided by the Federal Court decisions in Yu,36 Li,37 and Zhang38 [54] Based of the totality of findings noted above, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China. CONCLUSION [55] The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim.
